metaDescription: A desktop platform that gives finance teams control over corporate cards while making it easy for employees to get reimbursed quickly.

hero.title: Treezor, Business Expense Management
hero.summary: A desktop platform that lets finance teams issue and govern corporate cards while giving employees a fast, low-friction way to get reimbursed.

blocks.html: Treezor wanted to expand its API-based services into a white-label expense management product that could be offered to corporate customers. Working with AAZZUR, we designed a B2B web platform covering corporate cards, reimbursements, expenses, and procurement.

As Lead Product Designer, I owned the end-to-end experience, from early wireframes and workflows through prototyping, usability testing, and final UI, while adapting the product to evolving business requirements and technical constraints.
The platform launched in beta, with usability testing validating the core journeys while longer-term product metrics continue to be tracked.

items.challenge: Limited oversight across teams until it's too late to act

items.goal: Approve expenses without it slowing down their day
items.challenge: Everything is manual and disconnected from actual spending

items.goal: Submit an expense and move on
items.challenge: Uploading receipts and tracking reimbursements takes too much effort

blocks.html: Employees wanted things to move fast and feel simple. Finance wanted to know exactly where the money was going. Lean too far toward speed and you lose control of spend; lean too far toward control and people go back to spreadsheets and email just to get things done.
These came from informal user interviews, plus a look at how Spendesk, Pleo, and Captio handle similar tradeoffs.

items.finding: Users wanted control when OCR made mistakes.
items.insight: Make every extracted field editable, with manual entry always available.

items.finding: Finance needed spending control before cards were used.
items.insight: Add manager-set card limits and usage restrictions before issuing the card.

items.finding: One-off purchases were happening outside approval flows.
items.insight: Combine procurement requests and virtual card creation into a single approved flow.

blocks.html: In each case, the goal was the same: let people move quickly, but keep finance able to step in if something looks off.

Cards were designed around giving finance control before money is spent. Managers can review requests, set usage rules and limits, and manage cards from one place, while reporting makes it easier to spot missing receipts or compliance issues after transactions happen.

Employees can submit out-of-pocket expenses and supporting documents with minimal effort. OCR speeds up expense entry while keeping extracted fields editable and manual entry available when needed. Expenses are grouped into reports for approval, and once approved, employees are reimbursed directly to their personal bank account.

blocks.text: Keeping one-off purchases within the approval flow

blocks.html: Procurement brings purchase approval and card ordering into the same flow. Employees submit the purchase details upfront, managers review the request, and once approved they can issue a card for the purchase directly, keeping one-off spending inside the governed process instead of pushing it into email or separate tools

blocks.text: Giving finance a company-wide view of spending

blocks.html: Managers can create separate accounts for teams and budgets, assign users, manage payment settings, and review transactions associated with each account. The admin dashboard brings this structure together with real-time spending data, helping finance monitor budgets, compare activity across teams and payment methods, and identify unusual spending patterns.

The design went through several iterations based on stakeholder feedback, evolving requirements, technical constraints, and usability testing. Beta testing showed strong user confidence and task success across key flows.

The hardest part wasn't designing for any single user — it was designing the seams between roles, where one person's convenience becomes another's risk. What surprised me most was how much trust came from giving users an escape hatch (manual entry, editable OCR) rather than trying to make automation perfect. Next, the focus shifts to validating these early signals against real usage data and tightening the procurement-to-card handoff based on manager feedback.
